extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP counsel, and practitioners interested in fee-shifting under Octane Fitness
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the legal standards, factual patterns, and district-court trends courts use to decide whether a patent case is "exceptional" under Octane Fitness and thus warrant an award of attorneys' fees. Includes examples of conduct courts find (or do not find) exceptional and statistical/docket trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octane Fitness standard: unreasonable conduct may be 'exceptional' even if not sanctionable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court instructed that 'sanctionable conduct is not the appropriate benchmark' and that a court may award fees 'in the rare case in which a party’s unreasonable conduct—while not necessarily independently sanctionable—is nonetheless so "exceptional" as to justify an award of fees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply this language directly: the focus is on unreasonable, exceptional conduct rather than only conduct that would meet a sanction standard. District courts must therefore assess whether conduct rises above ordinary litigation behavior to the level of exceptional under Octane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances / flexible, case-specific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts engage in a totality-of-the-circumstances, flexible inquiry when deciding whether a case is exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider multiple facts and context-specific evidence rather than a rigid checklist. The movant's conduct and the other party's conduct are both relevant; courts look at the overall course of the litigation. Recovery is most likely when a pattern outside the realm of the typical case can be shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare conduct to ordinary/typical patent litigation tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts evaluate the tactics employed in the case at issue against what district courts perceive to be ordinary or typical in patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive litigation strategies are often viewed as inherent in patent litigation (e.g., 'hotly contested', 'par for the course'). Conduct that is common in high-stakes competitor litigation is less likely to be deemed exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material impact on the case required (no significant impact → likely not exceptional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that had no significant impact on the outcome or did not lead to any material activity in the litigation is less likely to be found exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even conduct described as 'obnoxious, and arguably unethical' may not justify a fee award if it did not materially affect the litigation. Courts emphasize the need to show some meaningful effect on the course or cost of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery disputes and motions to compel are generally not exceptional by themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery disputes and motions to compel are common in nearly all patent cases and alone do not amount to unreasonable or exceptional conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague allegations of discovery concealment or lack of transparency are unlikely to suffice. Courts have described 'bitter discovery disputes' as 'par for the course' and routinely deny motions for reconsideration when the conduct is simply typical dispute practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement offers/strategies alone are insufficient absent evidence of nuisance-value settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of low or even unreasonable settlement offers by itself is typically not grounds for a fees award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If settlement behavior evidences a strategy of pursuing nuisance-value settlements (e.g., many actions combined with settlements right before merits determinations), courts are more likely to find the conduct supports an exceptional-case finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both parties' conduct is relevant; movant must have 'clean hands'
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider the conduct of both parties; a movant's own bad acts or unreasonable conduct can prevent an award of attorneys' fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include instances where the accused infringer's misconduct led the court to deny the movant's request. Courts may attribute fault to both sides for excessive motion practice or dilatory tactics and decline to award fees on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of conduct that prolongs litigation, increases costs, or wastes judicial resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are willing to find exceptional conduct when a party's overall strategy was to prolong litigation, drive up costs, or needlessly complicate proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact patterns supporting awards include strategies forcing the opponent to 'expend large amounts of money in a lengthy and protracted litigation,' repeatedly arguing rejected positions, ignoring court orders, or unduly complicating the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to comply with court orders, failure to appear, and habitual procedural non-compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to comply with court orders, failing to appear in court, and routinely filing untimely or procedurally non-compliant papers are conduct likely to contribute to a finding of exceptionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cite these behaviors as indicia of unreasonable litigation conduct that can justify fee-shifting when they materially affect the litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive motion practice with no legitimate purpose (burden and delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive motion practice that appears to have 'no legitimate purpose' other than to burden or delay the other side tends to support a fee award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether motion practice served a legitimate litigation aim. Repeated, baseless, or dilatory motions that waste time and resources weigh in favor of finding the case exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing inaccurate records, misrepresentations, and deceptive acts (e.g., purposeful redactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing inaccurate records, making misrepresentations to the court or opposing party, or engaging in deceptive acts such as purposeful redaction to conceal material information are conduct that may justify fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct undermines the integrity of litigation and is specifically identified in decisions as likely to contribute to an award when it materially harms the adjudicative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gamesmanship and lack of good-faith cooperation (specific tactical examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gamesmanship and failure to act in good faith—such as filing dismissals/covenants without notifying opposing counsel on critical days, failing to explore settlement, premature summary-judgment filings followed by late withdrawals, or changing infringement theories without amending contentions—can support a determination of exceptionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists concrete examples courts have relied on: filing a dismissal/covenant on the day pretrial submissions were due without notice; not exploring settlement before/after an inter partes review; withdrawing declarations after the opponent incurred expense; and dropping patents late (Hatch-Waxman example where dropping patents two days before trial supported fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and circumstances of claim/claim-withdrawal conduct (pre-trial dropping of claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining numerous asserted claims until shortly before trial and then dropping patents or claims without warning (particularly close to trial) can be unreasonable, prejudicial, and reflective of substantive weakness—supporting fees in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The District of Delaware Hatch-Waxman example: maintaining 35 asserted claims until two weeks before trial and then dropping patents two business days before trial was found 'unreasonable, prejudicial' and supported a fees award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default judgments and their statistical effect on grant rates
rubrics_metrics.description: When defendants default, patent holders’ motions for exceptional-case fees have a significantly higher grant rate (example: 84% in defaults), which skews raw success statistics for patent holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics matter for practitioners evaluating likelihood of success; removing defaults reduces patent-holder prevail rate to approximately 32% in the sample discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: District/docket variance influences outcomes (location matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant rates and the frequency of exceptional-case decisions vary by district; nearly half of recent decisions came from five patent-intensive dockets (E.D. Tex., C.D. Cal., N.D. Cal., D. Del., S.D.N.Y.), and districts show different grant-rate trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware of local-docket tendencies: e.g., C.D. Cal. and N.D. Cal. saw grant-rate increases (44% and 56% respectively in the period), while other districts saw declines. Local practice and judges' tendencies can therefore affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery most likely when there is a demonstrable pattern outside the typical case plus material impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are most likely to award fees where the movant can point to a pattern of conduct outside the realm of the typical case and demonstrate that the conduct had a material impact on the course of the litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines the need to show atypicality and materiality: isolated, common, or immaterial bad acts are less persuasive than a demonstrable pattern causing increased costs or delay.
